concept.title: Graph Coloring with Emotions: The Chromatic Polynomial Meets Psychology
concept.concept_description: The chromatic polynomial chi_G(k) counts the number of proper k-colorings of a graph G. For a friendship graph, chi_G(k) counts the number of ways to assign k emotions to people such that no two friends share the same emotion. Conjecture: The chromatic polynomial evaluated at k=6 (for the 6 basic emotions: happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, surprise) gives the number of 'emotionally consistent' assignments of emotions to a social network. The chromatic polynomial has a root at k=2 for any bipartite graph, meaning a social network that splits cleanly into two groups has exactly 0 ways to assign 2 emotions without friends sharing emotions. The real emotional chromatic number chi_E(G) of a social network G is the smallest k such that chi_G(k) > 0 and k >= 3 (since real emotions need at least 3 categories to avoid trivial assignments). For a complete graph K_n (a clique of n mutual friends), chi_E(K_n) = n (everyone needs a different emotion). For a cycle C_n (a circular friendship chain), chi_E(C_n) = 2 if n is even and 3 if n is odd (alternating emotions work for even cycles, but odd cycles need a third emotion). Test: compute chi_E(G) for 100 real social networks and verify that the emotional chromatic number is between 3 and 6 for most networks. Impact: the chromatic polynomial is not just combinatorics — it measures the emotional diversity of a social network.

concept.lean_guess: Define the emotional chromatic number chi_E(G) = min{k >= 3 : chi_G(k) > 0}. For a graph G with n vertices and m edges, compute chi_G(k) using the deletion-contraction recurrence: chi_G(k) = chi_{G-e}(k) - chi_{G/e}(k). For social networks: the emotional chromatic number is the minimum number of emotions needed to ensure no two friends share the same emotion. For a complete graph K_n: chi_E = n (every person needs a different emotion). For a cycle C_n: chi_E = 2 if n even, 3 if n odd (but chi_E >= 3, so for even cycles chi_E = 3 by the minimum constraint). For a path P_n: chi_E = 3 (alternating two emotions doesn't satisfy k >= 3). For random graphs G(n, p): chi_E is approximately max(3, n / (2*log(n/p))) by the chromatic number asymptotics. Test: compute chi_E for 100 social networks from SNAP or similar databases. Verify: most social networks have chi_E between 3 and 6. The 6 basic emotions (Ekman) provide a natural upper bound.

concept.title: The Berggren Tree Zeta Function — Analytic Counting of Pythagorean Triples Governed by the Silver Ratio
concept.concept_description:
**Domain**: Pythagorean <-> NumberTheory

**Hypothesis**: The distribution of hypotenuses (and legs) over the Berggren ternary tree of primitive Pythagorean triples is governed by an exactly computable analytic object — a "tree zeta function" — whose abscissa of convergence and pole structure are determined by the silver ratio log(1+√2) growth exponent already proven for the tree. The conjecture: the Dirichlet series Σ_{triples in tree} c^{-s} (summed over the hypotenuse c of each node, or over the nodes at depth n with their growth) has an abscissa of convergence computable from the silver ratio, and the count of nodes with hypotenuse ≤ H satisfies an exact asymptotic law with an explicit exponent.

**Test**: Formalize the depth-n layer of the Berggren tree (3ⁿ nodes) and the distribution of hypotenuses within it. Define the tree zeta function and prove its abscissa of convergence is governed by the silver-ratio growth exponent. Prove an asymptotic law for the number of Berggren-generated triples with hypotenuse ≤ H (the catalog already has the Θ(H) count of Berggren-generated triples vs. H³ total — sharpen this to an exact asymptotic with the silver-ratio exponent). Relate the zeta function to the known spectral structure of the generators (eigenvalues 3±2√2).

**Why now**: The catalog has exact metric growth (silver speed limit), exact counting (Θ(H) Berggren-generated triples), and spectral classification — but no analytic-number-theory object tying them together. A tree zeta function would unify the growth, counting, and spectral results into a single analytic object, connecting to the theory of zeta functions of graphs, trees, and dynamical systems.

**If true**: The Berggren tree acquires a zeta function with a silver-ratio abscissa of convergence, unifying its growth, counting, and spectral structure — a clean analytic-number-theory companion to the existing geometric and algebraic results, with connections to Ihara zeta functions and the zeta functions of trees.

**If false**: The Dirichlet series fails to have a meromorphic continuation or its abscissa is not the silver ratio, which is itself a sharp statement about the analytic structure of the tree's counting function.

concept.title: Higher-Dimensional Pythagorean Trees — Generalizing the Berggren Tree to Pythagorean Quadruples and Hyperspheres
concept.concept_description:
**Domain**: Pythagorean <-> Geometry

**Hypothesis**: The Berggren ternary tree of primitive Pythagorean triples is the 2-dimensional case of a general family of trees of primitive Pythagorean n-tuples (solutions of x₁²+…+xₙ² = y²). For each n ≥ 3 there is a higher-dimensional "Pythagorean tree" generated by a finite set of Lorentz-preserving integer matrices acting on the null cone of the (n+1)-dimensional Lorentz form, generalizing the three Berggren moves. The conjecture: for n = 3 (Pythagorean quadruples / hyperspheres) there is a finite generating set of integer matrices, the tree has a well-defined hyperbolic embedding in the (n+1)-dimensional Poincaré ball, and its metric growth exponent is an exactly computable algebraic number generalizing the silver ratio log(1+√2).

**Test**: Formalize the null cone of the (n+1)-dimensional Lorentz form and the group of its integral Lorentz-preserving automorphisms. For n = 3, exhibit a finite generating set of matrices producing a tree of primitive Pythagorean quadruples, prove the tree's branching structure (how many children per node), and compute the hyperbolic metric growth exponent. Generalize the Berggren groupoid, the star-line structure, and the totient law to the higher-dimensional setting.

**Why now**: The entire existing corpus is the 2-dimensional Berggren tree. Higher-dimensional Pythagorean trees (quadruples, quintuples, hyperspheres) are a natural, essentially unexplored generalization that would extend the groupoid, hyperbolic-geometry, and growth machinery to a whole family of objects — and hypersphere packing / kissing-number questions give it concrete applications.

**If true**: A full higher-dimensional theory of Pythagorean trees emerges — groupoid, hyperbolic embedding, silver-ratio-type growth — generalizing the Berggren tree and connecting to sphere packing, quadratic forms in higher dimensions, and the arithmetic of the higher Lorentz groups.

**If false**: The higher-dimensional tree fails to be a clean ternary tree (e.g., branching grows with n, or the growth exponent is not algebraic), which itself characterizes how the beautiful 2-dimensional structure fails to generalize.
